summary: Orient Long Beach Bar Light, 'Bug Light': an 1871 screw-pile light off Orient, burned in 1963 and rebuilt as a working replica in 1990.

structures.note: Screw-pile house with an octagonal tower; burned 4 July 1963.
Working replica built at Greenport Yacht and Shipbuilding and set on the old concrete foundation.

access.note: Best seen by boat, according to LighthouseFriends; the tower and dwelling are closed.

facts.agency: East End Seaport Museum & Marine Foundation

events.note: Tower established 1871 per the archive; the museum says the original was built in 1870; the Suffolk Times says 1871.
Ice floe in Orient Harbor; the light was deserted and the ice started the piles on the west side (New York Herald, 13 March 1872).
Ice packed under the house and broke three pilings and nearly all the braces (keeper report as LighthouseFriends quotes it).
Board committee used the station as shore station for candle-power tests of running lights, 13 August 1890 (report covers the fiscal year ended 30 June 1891).
Fog-bell striking machine disabled by a falling weight; signal discontinued 18 March 1899 and resumed 22 June 1899.
Lower boat landing rebuilt and 400 tons of riprap placed to protect the station.
Steamer Shinnecock ran aground in fog in front of the station, 3 August 1911.
Assistant keeper John A. Miller capsized in a sailboat on 30 December 1911; the crew of the oyster dredge Cupid drew him aboard.
Concrete foundation and general repairs completed in fiscal 1922, $5,742. LighthouseFriends dates the concrete foundation to 1926.
Hurricane flooded the first floor; per the Suffolk Times the keeper and his grandson survived on the second floor.
Discontinued 1948 (archive); the sandbar had moved so far beyond the light that it was useless as a channel marker (LighthouseFriends).
Put up for sale by the federal government and auctioned; the Orient Point Marine Historical Association won with $1,710 (LighthouseFriends) or $1,700 (Suffolk Times).
Fire destroyed the building on the night of 4 July 1963. LighthouseFriends says arsonists set it; the Suffolk Times says some said arson and some said accident.
Working replica built at Greenport Yacht and Shipbuilding; moved onto the old foundation on 5 September 1990.
Coast Guard recognized the beacon as a federal aid to navigation.
Two local groups that had feuded over control signed an agreement to divide maintenance and repair work and to raise money together.

corrections.why: The standing tower in the record is the 1990 working replica. The 1871 tower was destroyed by fire in 1963, and the record already lists it as lost.
The 1963 entry describes the fire that destroyed the building, not a deactivation.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The museum gives 1870, and Congress funded the light in July 1870 (LighthouseFriends). The archive, LighthouseFriends (first lit 1 December 1871) and the Suffolk Times all give 1871 for the tower, so the story uses 1871 and notes the museum date.

The record has 1963 (from Wikidata) and the archive has 1948. The station was discontinued in 1948 (archive, LighthouseFriends, Suffolk Times); the building burned in 1963. Both dates are in the events list.

notes_for_editor: 1) Height: the archive gives 53 ft above mean high water (about 16.2 m, used as focal_height_m). LighthouseFriends says 54 ft, the museum says the replica light sits 63 ft above the water, and the record has 17.7 m (ENC). Check the Coast Guard Light List before publishing a figure. 2) Characteristic: the record says Fl W 4s; the Suffolk Times says the light later showed a white flash every five seconds. Left out of facts pending the Light List. 3) Range of 8 nautical miles comes only from the record; no source we read confirms it, so it is left out. 4) Concrete foundation: LighthouseFriends dates it to 1926; the Commissioner's fiscal 1922 summary lists a concrete foundation and general repairs as completed. The story gives both. 5) Auction: winning bid $1,710 (LighthouseFriends) or $1,700 (Suffolk Times); other bids $52 to $212 or about $200. The story gives both. 6) Roster: the archive lists Thompson (1871), Cornelius Oakes (1871-1872) and Thompson again (1872); LighthouseFriends gives one Thompson stint to April 1872 with no Oakes. The archive has George M. Fenton as assistant 1872-1873 where LighthouseFriends has George W. Fenton; and Jonathan S. Als where LighthouseFriends has John S. Als. Roster lines were checked against roster.py output (all 37 lines, person slugs included). 7) Fenton relationship: LighthouseFriends calls Charles M. Fenton the son of George M. Fenton. The archive does not state the relationship, so the story attributes it to LighthouseFriends. 8) OCR, Herald 13 March 1872 (cite 6): the day of the desertion is not clear from the OCR, so the story says only 'on a Saturday morning' in the quote; the OCR reads the correspondent's place as 'Oreeuport' (read as Greenport) and the phrase 'still nlihout a keeper' as 'still without a keeper'. The page image was not checked for these two words. The steamer's report is paraphrased from the OCR line 'The steamer Kscort reports night of llth that the bulldln | Is all right'. 9) OCR, Tribune 12 June 1872 (cite 5): the $20,000 sits on the OCR line 'Completing light-house at Long Beach Bar, Gardiner Bay, L. I. ... 20,000' under the sundry civil expenses heading; read from the OCR text, not the page image. 10) Fiscal years: the 1891 candle-power test is dated 13 August 1890, since the report covers the fiscal year ended 30 June 1891. The 1901 boat-landing work is dated to the fiscal year ended 30 June 1901, not to a calendar year. Printed page for scan 295 was not confirmed (scan page cited). 11) Commissioner FY1915 (cite 10): checked against the page image (scan 66, printed p. 61). It is a table titled 'Saving of Life and Property by Vessels or Employees of the Lighthouse Service during the Fiscal Year 1915', not a station roll. The Ehrhardt and Hamilton entry is matched by its row in the employee column (matched by position, with the vessel column not used); the story uses only the keeper and assistant keeper named there. 12) The 1938 hurricane account is from the Suffolk Times (2022), with the keeper unnamed; no contemporary report read. The 1963 fire date is in three sources, but no newspaper or official report was read for it. 13) Wikipedia was used only as a lead; its 1945 and 1963 deactivation dates and 58 ft height are not cited. 14) Not checked: the 1870-1872 first-lit and appropriation dates against the Lighthouse Board's own report of 1871-1872 (not in the corpus); the Coast Guard Light List; the 1948 discontinuance in newspapers. The December 1869 Herald plea is read as LighthouseFriends quotes it; the Herald itself was not read. 15) Newspaper searches: 1870-1873 (21 pages; 3 read); 1911-1912 'Long Beach Bar' with 'keeper' or 'lighthouse' (0 hits). 16) Living people: no one named after about 1960 except Merlon E. Wiggin, named by LighthouseFriends as leading the 1990 fundraising campaign in a public role; the museum's chairman is named in the Suffolk Times but not in the story. 17) John A. Miller's later service (four other stations, retirement from Montauk Point in 1943 per LighthouseFriends) is not in other_stations because the other stations are not named. 18) Verification 2026-10-27: first-run quote check found all 106 quotes (none missing). Changes: 'reached by boat only' and 'closest point on land' removed (LighthouseFriends says best seen by boat, with a land approach from Orient Point State Park); 'one difficult' corrected to 'only difficult'; fiscal-year wording for 1901; the 1915 table described as the employee table it is; a fuller 1872 Herald account including the steamer report; footnote 10 title corrected; the Fenton and 1911 wording closer to the sources.
